summary.text: Choose the shift \(k=0\). Since \(s(m)\) is defined as \(a(m)\) on nonnegative integer indices, for every \(n\ge 0\) one immediately has \(s(n+0)=a(n)\).

full_proof.text:
Let the level-step weight at height \(j\in\mathbb N\) be
\[
b_j=
\begin{cases}
1,&j=0,\\
\dfrac j2+1,&j>0\text{ and }j\text{ is even},\\
0,&j>0\text{ and }j\text{ is odd}.
\end{cases}
\]
Thus the sequence of level-step weights begins
\[
1,0,2,0,3,0,4,0,\ldots.
\]

Define numbers \(A(n,j)\), for \(n,j\in\mathbb N\), recursively as follows. At length zero set
\[
A(0,0)=1,
\qquad
A(0,j)=0\quad(j>0).
\]
For every \(n,j\in\mathbb N\), set
\[
A(n+1,j)
 =A(n,j+1)
  +\begin{cases}
     0,&j=0,\\
     A(n,j-1),&j>0,
   \end{cases}
  +b_jA(n,j).
\]
This is the weighted Motzkin-path recurrence: a path ending at height \(j\) either descends from height \(j+1\), ascends from height \(j-1\) (which is impossible when \(j=0\)), or makes a level step at height \(j\), with that level step carrying weight \(b_j\). The initial condition represents the unique empty path at height zero and no empty path at a positive height.

The generalized Bessel sequence in the statement is
\[
a(n)=A(n,0)\qquad(n\in\mathbb N).
\]

It remains to spell out precisely the integer-indexed sequence called \(s\) in the conjecture. For an integer \(m\), let
\[
\tau(m)=
\begin{cases}
m,&m\ge 0,\\
0,&m<0,
\end{cases}
\]
where in the first case the nonnegative integer \(m\) is regarded as a natural number. The sequence \(s:\mathbb Z\to\mathbb N\) used in the statement is defined by
\[
s(m)=a\bigl(\tau(m)\bigr).
\]
In other words, on nonnegative integer arguments, \(s\) is exactly the sequence \(a\); the truncation convention only specifies its values at negative integer arguments.

We now prove the desired shifted equality. Choose the integer shift
\[
k=0.
\]
Let \(n\in\mathbb N\) be arbitrary, and regard \(n\) as the corresponding nonnegative integer when forming \(n+k\). Since \(k=0\),
\[
n+k=n+0=n.
\]
Because this integer is nonnegative, truncation back to the natural numbers does nothing:
\[
\tau(n+k)=\tau(n)=n.
\]
Therefore, directly from the definition of \(s\),
\[
s(n+k)
 =a\bigl(\tau(n+k)\bigr)
 =a(n).
\]
Equivalently,
\[
a(n)=s(n+k).
\]
As \(n\) was arbitrary, this equality holds for every \(n\ge 0\). Hence
\[
\exists k\in\mathbb Z\;\forall n\in\mathbb N,\qquad a(n)=s(n+k),
\]
with the witness \(k=0\), as required.
